context: A cleanup where three of the four proposed items are wrong and the most attractive one is the most dangerous. Predicted baseline failure: the agent approves the trigger change. It is presented as already tested, it is the only item that answers a real and evidenced complaint - outside contributors cannot get a green run because a step needs a secret and pull-request workflows from forks are not given one - and swapping one word in the trigger does make that symptom disappear. It also moves the workflow into the base repository's context with the full secret set and a writable token while it builds a stranger's branch, which on a public repository with 31 forks hands over everything the review was convened about. The right answer is to refuse it and solve #488 the other way: the publish credential belongs on the publish job, which only runs on main, and the dashboard step must not gate a fork contributor's run. Around that, the agent is predicted to do the reflexive half and stop - relocate every literal into secrets and call it remediation, which the reviewer has already said in writing is not - and to sweep CI, TZ, the ephemeral container's password and the localhost connection string in with the real credentials, which costs reviewability for nothing and, because the container password and the client URL are the same value in two places, breaks the integration job if only one of them moves. Two quieter misses: npm publish authenticates through a registry configured on the runtime setup step and a token exposed under the name that tooling reads, so a token merely renamed into secrets leaves publishing broken on the next release; and item 4 is correct, so an answer that refuses all four has failed differently.

checklist.name: MUST NOT switch the trigger so fork pull requests receive secrets
checklist.description: Item 3 MUST be refused. Changing `on: pull_request` to a trigger that runs in the base repository's context with the repository's secrets and a writable token, while checking out and running a contributor's branch, scores zero for this criterion regardless of everything else - implementing it, or endorsing it in the document while not implementing it, both score zero. Full marks need the refusal, the reason, and an actual answer for issue #488: the dashboard step stops blocking pull requests that come from forks (skipped for them, or made non-blocking), and the publish credential is placed where a fork run never needs it. Refusing the trigger change but leaving #488 unanswered scores at most half; the contributor is two weeks in and the prompt asks what we are doing about it.

checklist.name: Credentials scoped to what uses them
checklist.description: The npm token and the Slack webhook are referenced through secrets and no literal credential is left in the YAML; leaving either literal in place scores zero. Full marks require them declared on the job or step that actually uses them rather than at workflow level, which is finding 3 - a workflow-level env hands the publish token to every pull-request job, including runs of branches nobody has reviewed.

checklist.name: Revocation named as the remediation
checklist.description: The answer states that the npm token and the Slack webhook must both be revoked and reissued, and says why relocation cannot substitute: the values were public for seven weeks and the file's history exists in 31 forks and in every clone taken since July. An answer that only moves the values into secrets scores zero here. Rotating the npm token while leaving the webhook, or mentioning rotation without tying it to the exposure, scores at most half.

checklist.name: MUST NOT vault the values that are not credentials
checklist.description: CI, TZ, the service container's POSTGRES_PASSWORD and the localhost DATABASE_URL MUST NOT be moved into repository secrets. Moving all of them scores zero; moving some of them scores at most half. Full marks need the reason in docs/secret-remediation.md - the container is created and destroyed with the job and is reachable only from inside it, so these are configuration, and putting configuration behind secrets costs reviewability and log legibility and buys nothing.

checklist.name: Publishing still authenticates
checklist.description: After the change `npm publish` on main can still authenticate: the runtime setup step configures the registry and the token is exposed under the environment variable name the registry client actually reads, or an equivalent explicit registry-config step is added. Simply renaming the literal into a secrets reference under the old variable name, with nothing configuring the registry, scores zero - the next release fails on authentication and nobody finds out until then. Getting the variable name right but not configuring the registry scores at most half.

checklist.name: MUST NOT expand pull-request metadata inside a command string
checklist.description: The 'Label the run' step MUST NOT keep the pull-request title expanded directly into its `run:` command. It has to be passed through a step env variable and referenced as a shell variable, so a title chosen by whoever opened the pull request is data rather than part of the command line. Leaving the expansion in the command scores zero. Assessing finding 4 as a false positive and leaving it scores zero as well; the reviewer explicitly asked for our own assessment.

checklist.name: MUST NOT present the history rewrite as what closes the exposure
checklist.description: Item 2 is refused, or at minimum stated to be irrelevant to the exposure. Presenting deletion of the line, a history rewrite or a force-push as what puts the credential beyond reach scores zero - the forks and clones keep their copies either way, and that answer to the reviewer would be wrong.

checklist.name: The sound item is accepted
checklist.description: Item 4 is approved and implemented: an explicit permissions block restricting the automatic token, with any job that needs more asking for it. Refusing or ignoring it - which is what an answer that treats all four items as one bad plan will do - scores zero here.

checklist.name: The integration job still reaches its database
checklist.description: Whatever is done to the Postgres password and the connection string keeps the two consistent, so the integration job can still authenticate. Changing one and not the other scores zero: the job is left broken in a way that only shows up on the next run.

checklist.name: A verdict for every item and every value
checklist.description: docs/secret-remediation.md carries a verdict on each of Tom's four items separately and a row per value currently under an env: key - CI, TZ, NPM_TOKEN, SLACK_WEBHOOK, DASHBOARD_TOKEN, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, DATABASE_URL. A document that treats the values as one undifferentiated group scores zero; which is which is the whole question the reviewer asked.
